summary: John Marshall worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He studied at Cambridge, the British School at Athens, and under Arthur Evans. He served as Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India (1902–1931) and Honorary Fellow at King's College, Cambridge (~1927–1958).
Working in religious and Buddhist studies, John Marston earned his PhD from the University of Washington in 1997. He held a post at El Colegio de México.

John Muir studied at Glasgow, the East India Company College, and Bonn. He served in the Bengal Civil Service (1828–1853), was principal of Sampurnanand Sanskrit University in 1844, founded the University of Edinburgh in 1862, and held a post there.
John Myrdhin Reynolds is a scholar in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He pursued traditional studies under Dudjom Rinpoche (~1974–1987) and Namkhai Norbu (~1976).

John Nemec is an Indology, religious studies, and philosophy scholar who studied at Rochester, UCSB, Oxford, and Penn (PhD 2005) under Alexis Sanderson and Ludo Rocher. He became Associate Professor of Indian Religions and South Asian Studies at the University of Virginia (attested 2020).
Linguist John Okell studied at The Queen's College, Oxford, and under Hla Pe, Anna J. Allott, and Richard Keith Sprigg. From 1959 to 1999, he was a research associate at SOAS University of London.

John P. Keenan studied Buddhist and religious studies under Minoru Kiyota at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (PhD attested 1980) and under Noriaki Hakamaya. He was a Research Fellow at Nanzan Institute (1983–1986) and Professor of Religion at Middlebury College (attested 1989–2006).

John Peile was a linguist and Indologist who studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, and under Theodor Benfey. He was Fellow and Tutor at Christ's College (~1860–1910), Reader at Cambridge (1884–1891), and president of Newnham College (~1890–1909).
John Pickford studied under Monier Monier-Williams and served as a professor at the University of Madras.

John Powers studied Buddhist studies and Tibetology at Holy Cross, McMaster, and Virginia (PhD ~1984–1991) under Jeffrey Hopkins and others. His posts include Australian National University (1995), Deakin University (2016–2022), and lecturer at the University of Melbourne (2022).

Working in Indology, Tibetology, and Buddhist studies, John R. B. Campbell completed his PhD at Columbia University under Robert A. F. Thurman and Gary A. Tubb. He also studied under Tenzin Gyatso, Denma Lochö Rinpoche, and several other teachers.

John R. McRae studied Buddhist studies and Sinology at Yale (PhD ~1975–1983) under Stanley Weinstein, and under Seizan Yanagida. He taught at Cornell (~1988–1995), Indiana University (~1996–2005), Soka University (2004), and Komazawa University (~2005–2008).

John Ronald Newman specialized in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and Indology, earning his PhD at the University of Wisconsin-Madison under Geshe Lhundub Sopa (-1987). He held posts at Wisconsin-Madison (attested 1987) and New College of Florida (attested 1996–2000).

Scholar of Buddhist and religious studies John Ross Carter studied at King's College London, SOAS, and Harvard (PhD ~1967–1972) under Wilfred Cantwell Smith. He served as a professor at Colgate University's Chapel House (~1972–2006).

John S. Strong studied Buddhist and religious studies at Oberlin, Hartford, and Chicago (PhD ~1972–1977) under Frank E. Reynolds and J. A. B. van Buitenen. He served at Bates College (~1978–2017) and held several visiting professorships.

Linguist and Indologist John Shakespear studied under John Richardson. He held professorships in oriental studies at the Royal Military College, Sandhurst (1805–1809) and the Addiscombe Military Seminary (1809–1829).
Active in Indology, history, and archaeology, John Shore succeeded William Jones and served as President of The Asiatic Society from ~1794 to 1797.

Indologist and religious studies scholar John Stratton Hawley studied at Amherst College and under Daniel H. H. Ingalls (~1971–1977). He held a post at Bowdoin College (~1975–1977) before becoming a professor at Columbia University (~1986).
Philosopher John Stuart Mill studied at University College London (~1828–1830) and held a post at the East India Company from ~1823 to 1858.

John Sydenham Furnivall worked in history and archaeology, studying at Cambridge (Trinity Hall and Trinity College) and Leiden University. He founded the Burma Research Society in 1910 and held a post at the University of Cambridge (~1936–1941).
